extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Worked examples and exercises about blow-ups (explicit descriptions, exceptional divisors, proper transforms, resolving singularities, effects on line bundles and canonical bundle, deformation to the normal cone) followed by the introductory construction and basic properties of the Tor derived functors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel of β (Lemma 22.3.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: The kernel of β is (L2, . . . , Ld) where Li := a1Ti − ai; proved by induction on d with base case d = 2 using the Remainder Theorem and the injectivity of A[a2/a1] and an inductive step via A' = A[a2/a1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline: for d=2 divide F(T2) by a1T2−a2 to get remainder R; substituting T2 = a2/a1 and injectivity shows R=0 so divisibility holds. For general d use A' = A[a2/a1], reduce to previous cases and use kernels of composed maps to identify the kernel as (L2,...,Ld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for coefficients lying in I in Theorem 22.3.8
rubrics_metrics.description: If a homogeneous polynomial F of degree n satisfies F(a1,...,ad)=0 (or lies in In+1), then the coefficients of F lie in (a1,...,ad)=I (equivalently F ∈ I A[X1,...,Xd]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to checking F(1, a2/a1, ..., ad/a1)=0 in A[a2/a1,...,ad/a1] and apply Lemma 22.3.12 to identify kernel generators; this shows the coefficients are in I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of the blow-up of A^2 at the origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Bl_{(0,0)} A^2 = Proj k[x,y,X,Y] with relation xY − yX = 0; using projective coordinates [X:Y] on P^1 with x,y degree 0 and X,Y degree 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on the two standard patches [X:Y]=[s:1] and [1:t], giving affine charts Spec k[x,y,s]/(sy−x) ≅ A^2 and Spec k[x,y,t]/(y−xt) ≅ A^2; both charts are smooth which shows the blow-up is smooth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional divisor description on blow-up charts
rubrics_metrics.description: On the s-patch the ideal (x,y) becomes (ys,y) = (y) so the exceptional divisor is cut out by y; on the t-patch it is cut out by x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the defining local equations differ on patches, they describe the same exceptional divisor globally; this explicit description is useful for computing multiplicities and intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper transform regularity for nodal and cuspidal curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up the origin of certain plane curve singularities (e.g., nodal cubic y^2 = x^3 + x^2 and cuspidal y^2 = x^3) yields a proper transform that is regular, with the proper transform meeting the exceptional divisor in points corresponding to tangent directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the equation on each patch (substitute coordinates like y = xs or y = xt), factor to see exceptional divisor multiplicity and the residual factor giving the proper transform; check smoothness directly in the chart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibit Bl_p P^2 ≅ Hirzebruch surface F1 (Exercise 22.4.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a k-point p in P^2, Bl_p P^2 is isomorphic to the Hirzebruch surface F1 = P_{P^1}(O ⊕ O(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the isomorphism explicitly using coordinates: informally view a point as the line connecting it to the origin; coordinate computations on patches show the required identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hironaka resolution remark (characteristic 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a variety over a field of characteristic 0, then X can be resolved by a sequence of blow-ups where each blow-up is along a regular subvariety contained in the singular locus of the previous stage (Hironaka's theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book indicates the 1- and 2-dimensional cases will be shown later; in positive characteristic analogous statements are not known in general but de Jong's alterations provide usable substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: blowing up nonreduced subschemes can create singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up a nonreduced subscheme of a regular scheme may yield a singular scheme (example: blowing up V(y, x^2) in Spec k[x,y] produces an A1 surface singularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume blow-ups of arbitrary subschemes of smooth schemes remain smooth; the subscheme being nonreduced or non-Cartier can cause singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blowing up resolves base locus of rational map to projective space (Exercise 22.4.L)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given Y, an invertible sheaf L, and sections s0,...,sn (a linear series) with base locus X (scheme-theoretic), the morphism defined away from X to P^n extends uniquely to a morphism Bl_X Y → P^n; the invertible sheaf giving this morphism is (β^* L)(−E_XY).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove it, work affine-locally where L is trivial; uniqueness can use exercises on maps from blow-ups (e.g., Exercise 11.4.G). The exceptional divisor EXY removes the base locus by 'dividing out' the common factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of a function at a regular point (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f a function on a locally Noetherian scheme X and p a regular point, the multiplicity mult_p f is the largest m such that f lies in the m-th power of the maximal ideal m_p ⊂ O_{X,p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: V(f) is singular at p iff mult_p f > 1. This multiplicity is used to compute exceptional divisor multiplicities in blow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of exceptional divisor in total transform (Exercise 22.4.J)
rubrics_metrics.description: When blowing up the origin, the multiplicity of the exceptional divisor in the total transform of a subscheme Z of A^n is the smallest multiplicity (at the origin) among defining equations of Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute examples: nodal and cuspidal curves both give exceptional divisor multiplicity 2 in the total transform; compare multiplicities of defining polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small resolutions and non-isomorphic small resolutions (Atiyah flop example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some resolutions (small resolutions) have fibers over singular points of codimension > 2r for fiber dimension r; the cone over a quadric admits small resolutions whose fibers over the cone point are P^1, and different small resolutions need not be isomorphic (Atiyah flop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve rational maps by blowing up appropriate base loci (possibly non-Cartier divisors); examine fibers and compare birational models to see examples of flops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of linear series under blow-up (22.4.9 remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulling back a linear series to Bl_X Y yields a linear series whose base locus is EXY, an effective Cartier divisor; dividing out EXY produces a base-point-free series corresponding to the resolved morphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret via universal property: blowing up is the minimal modification removing the base locus; if X is already Cartier one can 'divide out' X without blowing up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact sequence for Pic of a blow-up (Exercise 22.4.O)
rubrics_metrics.description: For β: Bl_p X → X with exceptional divisor E, there is an exact sequence Z [E] → Pic(Bl_p X) → Pic(Bl_p X  ackslash E) → 0 and in the regular projective surface case Pic(Bl_p X) ≅ Pic X ⊕ Z with β^* giving a section; O_X(E)|_E ≅ O_E(−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the identification Pic = Cl for regular local rings, and exercise 13.8.5 and 15.4.15 for technical steps; calculate intersections using N^1 and pullbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback formula for Cartier divisors under blow-up (Exercise 22.4.P)
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is an effective Cartier divisor on X and mult_p D is its multiplicity at p, and D^~ is the proper transform, then π^* D = D^~ + (mult_p D) E as effective Cartier divisors; consequently π^* O_X(D) ≅ O_{Bl_p X}(D^~) ⊗ O_{Bl_p X}(E)^{mult_p D}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show locally that the product of the local equation of D^~ and the mult_p D-th power of a local equation for E equals a local equation for π^* D; this yields the structural isomorphism of line bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of canonical bundle under blow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: For π : Bl_{p} Y → Y with p a regular point on a smooth variety of dimension n, K_{Bl_p Y} ≅ (π^* K_Y) ⊗ O((n−1)E). More generally, blowing up a smooth m-dimensional subvariety Z of a smooth n-dimensional Y gives K_X ≅ (β^* K_Y) ⊗ O((n−m−1)E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute on local charts (e.g., for A^2 blow-up use coordinates y = m x to see pullback dx ∧ dy vanishes to order 1 along E); exercise 22.4.R and 22.4.S guide the generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensional cohomology vanishing for quasiprojective schemes (22.4.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasiprojective k-variety X of dimension n can be covered by n+1 affine open subsets, and therefore for any quasi-coherent sheaf F on X, H^i(X,F) = 0 for i > n (extension of Theorem 18.2.6 to quasiprojective schemes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed X in a projective Y of the same dimension, blow up the complement to make it an effective Cartier divisor, and restrict an affine cover of Y' to X; note that not every variety of dimension n has an n+1 affine cover (counterexamples are non-quasiprojective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformation to the normal cone (Exercise 22.4.U)
rubrics_metrics.description: For closed subscheme X ⊂ Y, the blow-up β : Bl_{X×{0}} (Y×A^1) → Y×A^1 gives a family whose fiber over 0 is the union of Bl_X Y and the projective completion of the normal cone to X in Y, and whose fiber over t ≠ 0 is canonically isomorphic to Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the exceptional divisor with the projective completion of the normal cone; the deformation is flat and is a key construction in modern intersection theory (Fulton–MacPherson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tor via resolutions (23.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an A-module M and a free (or projective) resolution R → N, Tor_i^A(M,N) is the i-th homology of the complex M ⊗_A R; Tor_0^A(M,N) ≅ M ⊗_A N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a free resolution of N (possibly infinite), truncate and tensor with M; although tensoring is only right-exact, the homology groups of the resulting complex define the Tor functors; proofs use homotopy invariance of the induced maps on homology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of Tor from chosen resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The groups Tor_i^A(M,N) are independent (canonically up to unique isomorphism) of the chosen free/projective resolution of N because any two lifts of a map of modules to resolutions are homotopic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show any two lifts of the identity map between resolutions are homotopic (exercise 23.1.A); use this to show maps induced on homology are independent of choices, giving well-defined functors Tor_i^A(M,·).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long exact sequence of Tor (Proposition 23.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a short exact sequence 0 → N' → N → N'' → 0 there is a long exact sequence ... → Tor_i^A(M,N') → Tor_i^A(M,N) → Tor_i^A(M,N'') → Tor_{i-1}^A(M,N') → ... → M⊗N'' → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by choosing resolutions of N' and N'' and assembling via the horseshoe construction to get a short exact sequence of resolutions, then tensor with M and take homology to obtain the long exact sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of flatness via Tor (Exercise 23.1.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an A-module M the following are equivalent: (i) M is flat; (ii) Tor_i^A(M,N) = 0 for all i > 0 and all A-modules N; (iii) Tor_1^A(M,N) = 0 for all A-modules N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fact that tensoring with M is right-exact and that vanishing of higher Tors precisely measures failure of exactness; this gives an equivalent homological criterion for flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective modules and lifting property (23.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A module P is projective iff for every surjection M → N and morphism P → N there exists a lift P → M, equivalently Hom_A(P, ·) is exact (left-exactness becomes exactness for projectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace free modules by projective modules throughout the Tor construction to compute Tor via projective resolutions; exercises show projective iff direct summand of a free module.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective modules are direct summands of free modules (Exercise 23.2.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module P is projective if and only if P is a direct summand of a free A-module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard algebra exercise: use the lifting property and split exact sequences; this justifies using projective resolutions in place of free ones when defining derived functors like Tor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on symmetry of Tor for i>0
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Tor_0^A(M,N) ≅ M ⊗_A N is symmetric in M and N, symmetry Tor_i^A(M,N) ≅ Tor_i^A(N,M) for i>0 is not immediate and is deferred to a later exercise (23.3.A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that many expected formal properties of derived functors require proofs; do not assume symmetry of higher Tor without verification.
